meta.description: Genuine Darwin. He wrote it to his sister Susan from Bahia on 4 August 1836, near the end of the Beagle voyage — in a private letter, not in any of his books.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A man who dares to waste one hour of time has not discovered the value of life'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Darwin wrote it to his sister Susan from Bahia, 4 August 1836. A private letter, not On the Origin of Species. See the manuscript and the 1887 printing.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and pinned to the manuscript: Darwin wrote it to his sister Susan from Bahia, Brazil, on 4 August 1836, on the Beagle’s homeward leg. The letter reads “…that a man who dares to waste one hour of time, has not discovered the value of life” — the popular version simply lifts that closing clause.

source.excerpt: I trust one part at least will turn out true, & that I shall act, as I now think.—that a man who dares to waste one hour of time, has not discovered the value of life.—
trail: The manuscript is transcribed at the Darwin Correspondence Project ↗ as letter DCP-LETT-306: Charles Darwin to Susan Elizabeth Darwin, Bahia, Brazil, 4 August 1836, autograph letter, DAR 223: 37.

Wikiquote ↗ carries it in its sourced section, citing The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (1887), volume I, chapter VI ‘The Voyage’, page 266, letter to sister Susan Elizabeth Darwin (4 August 1836).
LibQuotes ↗ gives the identical citation — volume I, chapter VI, page 266, letter to Susan Elizabeth Darwin, 4 August 1836.
The volume itself is free to read at Darwin Online ↗: Francis Darwin, ed., The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin, Including an Autobiographical Chapter, vol. I (London: John Murray, 1887).
source.excerptNote: Darwin’s own spelling and punctuation, from the Darwin Correspondence Project’s transcription of the manuscript. The line that circulates today is the closing clause, with the comma after ‘time’ dropped and ‘that a man’ raised to ‘A man’.

source.rightsNote: Darwin wrote the letter in 1836, and it appeared in Francis Darwin’s The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (London: John Murray, 1887). Both the writing and the first printing predate 1931 by decades, so the text is in the public domain in the United States. Written in English, so no translation rights attach.

author.name: Charles Darwin
author.heading: About Charles Darwin
author.bio: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist and geologist who sailed as ship’s naturalist aboard HMS Beagle between 1831 and 1836; the observations he gathered on that voyage underpinned On the Origin of Species (1859). He was also a relentless letter-writer, and a great deal of what we know about his thinking survives in correspondence with family, mentors and fellow scientists rather than in his published books. This line comes from that private side of him — a note home to his older sister Susan, written months before the ship reached England.

misattribution.heading: The attribution is right. The sourcing usually is not.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous-name quotes that survives checking — Darwin really wrote it. What goes wrong is everything around it: where it came from, when, and how much of the sentence you are actually reading.

items.why: Large aggregators print the line over a portrait with nothing attached — Quotefancy ↗ gives “— Charles Darwin” and no book, letter or date. That is how a hedged sentence from a private 1836 letter ends up reading like a corporate motto.

AZQuotes ↗ cites it to Charles Darwin and Francis Darwin, Autobiography and Selected Letters (1958), p. 145 — a twentieth-century reprint of an abridged Victorian selection. The words were written in 1836 and reached print in Francis Darwin’s 1887 Life and Letters.

items.who: Darwin the author, rather than Darwin the letter-writer
items.why: It is not from On the Origin of Species or the Journal of Researches. It is family correspondence: the Darwin Correspondence Project ↗ transcribes it from the autograph letter, DAR 223: 37, written at Bahia.

Darwin wrote “…that a man who dares to waste one hour of time, has not discovered the value of life” — a clause inside a resolution he was making about his own future. The circulating form drops the comma, raises “that a man” to “A man”, and cuts the hedge in front of it. See the manuscript transcription ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Darwin really wrote it, on 4 August 1836, to his sister Susan — Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ cites it to The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin (1887), vol. I, ch. VI ‘The Voyage’, p. 266.

context.heading: A young man talking himself into a working life
lead: Darwin wrote the line near the end of the Beagle’s five-year circuit, from Bahia in Brazil, replying to family news that the Cambridge geologist Adam Sedgwick had praised the collections he had been shipping home — a letter you can read in full at the Darwin Correspondence Project ↗. He is not lecturing anyone about productivity. He is talking himself into a working life.

The sentence that follows him around is the tail of a longer, more tentative thought: he hopes that one part at least of what has been said about him will turn out true, and resolves to act on the belief that comes next. Two months later he was writing to Captain FitzRoy from Shrewsbury, home from the voyage ↗ on 6 October 1836.
detailsBody: In the manuscript the thought runs on: “I trust one part at least will turn out true, & that I shall act, as I now think.—that a man who dares to waste one hour of time, has not discovered the value of life.—” The clause is a resolution he is making about himself, hedged with “I trust” and “as I now think”.
Detached and re-capitalised as “A man who dares…”, it becomes a universal rule addressed to the reader. The words are Darwin’s; the finger-wagging is the internet’s.
context.pull: “I trust one part at least will turn out true, & that I shall act, as I now think.”
